newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's Kokh urges postponment of Norilsk tender.
newsitem.headline: Russia's Kokh urges postponment of Norilsk tender.

text.p: Russia's top privatisation official urged government representatives due to vote on results of a tender for 38 percent of mining group Norilsk Nickel on Tuesday to put off the tender for an unspecified period.

The outcome of the vote is still far from certain, although the make-up of the commission which will decide the fate of the controversial tender would appear to support commercial bank Uneximbank in its high-profile bid for the company.

State Property Committee head Alfred Kokh's press secretary Viktoria Vergelskaya said Kokh had instructed three government representatives taking part in the decision to vote against announcing the winner on Tuesday as originally planned.
"Yes, Kokh instructed the state representatives in the commission to vote for delaying the sale (of the Norilsk stake)," Vergelskaya told Reuters.
The commission, which has just started its deliberations, comprises six people.
As well as the three government representatives, there will be one person from the Norilsk group, one from Uneximbank, and one from the tender commissioner, MFK Moscow Partners.
Norilsk has said it supports Uneximbank's bid, and MFK- Moscow Partners is linked to MFK Bank (IFCI in English), which is the investment arm of commercial bank Uneximbank.
The composition of the commission would therefore appear to pit three votes against three, making the deciding vote, which goes to the chairman commission, crucial.

Sources at the commission would not confirm who the chairman is, but Uneximbank's Chernitsyn said it would normally be the company who had control of shares in whatever company was being sold or the commissioner, in this case MFK Moscow Partners.

"Practice shows that the chairman is normally the controller of the shares-for-loans stake or the commissioner," he said. But he was unable to confirm whether this was in fact the case in this instance.
Uneximbank won control of the 38 percent stake in Norilsk, which represents 51 percent of voting rights, in 1995 under the shares-for-loans scheme.
If normal practice prevails, the vote looks set to go in favour of Uneximbank. But such is the political pressure on organisers of the tender to postpone or suspend it, nothing is certain.

Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin on Monday instructed the Russian State Property Committee (Russia's privatisation ministry) and the Federal Property Fund, both representing the government in the vote, to suspend the sale. The third state representative is from the Finance Ministry.
Critics of the tender say that Uneximbank has had an unfair advatage over other pretenders.
The winner of the stake has to invest $300 million in developing a gas deposit which will be used to fuel the group's main production plant, called the Norilsk combine.
Norilsk is the world's largest palladium producer, one of the world's biggest platinum and nickel suppliers, and a major producer of copper and cobalt.
Debts of around $70 million must also be paid off, with the starting price of the shares costing at least another 131.61 million Ecus.
